title: Batch on one machine: pipes, sorting and hashing
goal: By the end you can read a Unix log pipeline as a map, a shuffle and a reduce, choose between hash aggregation and an external merge sort from the number of distinct keys, and work out the runs and merge passes a sort needs for a given buffer and fan-in.

warmup.q: A 500 GB log has about 2 billion distinct idempotency keys. Your laptop has 16 GB of RAM and a 1 TB SSD. Which way of counting each key's lines can finish?
options: A Kotlin HashMap from key to count, if you give the JVM 15 GB of heap
`sort | uniq -c`, because sort writes sorted runs to disk and merges them
Neither: anything bigger than RAM needs a cluster
warmup.why: A hash map must hold every distinct key until the end: 2 billion entries at about 100 bytes each is around 200 GB, far more than 15 GB of heap. A sort only needs a buffer: it sorts chunks that fit, writes them as runs, and merges the runs with a few files open at once. It needs disk space for the runs and gets slower as the input grows, but it doesn't run out of memory. Bigger than RAM isn't the line for a cluster; bigger than one machine's disks or deadline is.

sections.h: Four small programs answer a question about a log
sections.body:
Lesson 1 sized batch jobs by the bytes they read. This lesson looks at what a job does with those bytes once it has them, on one machine, before any cluster gets involved.

Your payments API writes one line per request to an access log. Here is one, in NGINX's combined format:

```text
10.0.22.243 - - [07/Nov/2026:00:00:00 +0000] "POST /v1/authorizations HTTP/1.1" 201 776 "-" "acquirer-sdk/4.2"
```

The on-call engineer asks which five paths got the most requests yesterday. The log has 2,000,000 lines, 231 MB. That is too much to read by eye and far too little to need a cluster. One line of shell answers it:

```bash
awk '{print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
```

Read it left to right. `awk '{print $7}'` splits each line on blanks and prints the seventh field, the path. `sort` puts the paths in order. `uniq -c` turns each run of equal lines into one line with a count in front. `sort -rn` orders those lines by the count, read as a number (`-n`), largest first (`-r`). `head -5` keeps the first five. The `|` between two programs is a **pipe**: the kernel connects one program's output to the next program's input, so lines flow from stage to stage without a file in between.

```text
 100759 /v1/authorizations
  59071 /v1/captures
  41915 /healthz
  32574 /v1/refunds
  26302 /v1/tokens
```

Why is the first `sort` there? Because `uniq` compares each line only with the one just before it. It never remembers older lines, so it can only count copies that sit next to each other. Leave the sort out and `/v1/authorizations` shows up on 95,760 separate output lines, most with a count of 1, because other paths keep coming in between. So the job has to bring equal keys together, and the first sort is how this pipeline does it. That one step is the expensive part of every batch job in this track, MapReduce and Spark included.

This is a **batch job**: it reads input that already exists and doesn't change while the job runs, and it computes its whole result from scratch each time. If the awk expression was wrong, you fix it and run again. The log is untouched, so a bad run costs only time. The rest of this lesson takes the job apart: why it is built from small programs, the two ways to bring equal keys together (a hash table or a sort), and what happens to each when the keys no longer fit in memory.

sections.h: Small programs, one interface, and the wiring kept apart
sections.body:
None of the five programs in that pipeline knows anything about access logs, or about each other. That is on purpose. Doug McIlroy, who proposed pipes at Bell Labs, wrote the style down in 1978 in the foreword to the Unix issue of the Bell System Technical Journal. Its first rule is "Make each program do one thing well." The second says to expect the output of every program to become the input of another program that doesn't exist yet.

The programs are small. `sort` sorts, `uniq` collapses runs, `head` stops early. Each is easy to test and to trust, and you combine them instead of writing a new program for every question.

They share one interface. Every program reads bytes from its standard input and writes bytes to its standard output, and by convention those bytes are lines of text with fields separated by blanks, so any program can feed any other. Change `$7` to `$9` and the same pipeline counts status codes; change it to `$1` and it counts client IP addresses.

And the wiring lives outside them. `awk` doesn't know whether its output goes to a file, a terminal or another program; the shell decides that. You can add a `tee` to keep a copy of the middle of the pipeline, or swap one stage, without touching the others.

Pipes also run the stages at the same time. Each program is its own process, and the kernel gives each pipe a small buffer, 64 KiB by default on Linux. When the buffer is full, the writer blocks until the reader catches up. That is **backpressure**: a slow stage slows the stages before it instead of filling memory. When `head` has its lines and exits, the program writing to it gets a SIGPIPE signal on its next write and stops, so `awk '{print $7}' access.log | head -3` returns almost at once.

The figure lines the pipeline up with MapReduce, the subject of the next lesson. `awk` is the **map** step: it turns each input record into a key. The first `sort` is the **shuffle**: it brings equal keys together. `uniq -c` is the **reduce** step: it walks each group of equal keys and emits one result. Ranking by count needs a second sort, and in MapReduce that is a second job. MapReduce kept the small composable steps, the uniform record format (key and value pairs instead of lines) and the rule that input is never changed. It replaced the pipe with files in a distributed file system and the local sort with a sort across machines. DDIA's second edition makes the same comparison: a batch framework on a cluster has the parts this one machine has, namely storage behind a file interface, a scheduler that runs programs, and a way to wire their inputs to their outputs.

sections.h: A hash map counts in one pass, until the keys outgrow memory
sections.body:
Sorting is not the only way to bring equal keys together. Version 1 of counting doesn't sort at all: keep a hash map from key to count, read each line once, and add one to its key's count. awk can do it in one line:

```bash
awk '{n[$7]++} END {for (p in n) print n[p], p}' access.log | sort -rn | head -5
```

In Kotlin it is a `HashMap<String, Long>` and `counts.merge(path, 1L, Long::plus)`. Each line costs one hash and one lookup. There is no sort and no disk, and the second `sort` only has to order the distinct paths, not two million lines. This is **hash aggregation**, and while it fits, nothing beats it.

What has to fit? Not the lines: the **distinct keys**. Counting the eight API endpoints over two million lines needs eight entries, a few hundred bytes. Counting raw paths is different, because every payment has its own page, `/v1/payments/pay_0556303`. The demo log has 351,305 distinct paths, and each one needs an entry that lives until the end of the job.

On the JVM an entry costs more than its key. There is the map's entry object, the `String` and the byte array inside it, a boxed `Long` for the count, and a slot in the map's table. The demo below measured about 111 bytes per entry for 24-byte paths on this laptop's JDK 25. So a million distinct paths take about 111 MB of heap, and 50 million distinct idempotency keys would take more than 5 GB.

Where it breaks, it breaks all at once. The same demo starts a JVM with a 64 MB heap and keeps adding new paths. It died with `OutOfMemoryError` after about 617,000 of them. The job doesn't slow down gently first; on a real service it spends its last minutes in garbage collection and then dies, usually near the end, after most of the work is done. And you can't fix it by reading more slowly, because the map has to hold every distinct key until the last line is read.

So the rule is to estimate the working set, distinct keys times bytes per entry, before you pick hashing. Counts by endpoint, status, merchant or currency almost always fit. Counts by card number, idempotency key or raw URL may not.

sections.h: Sorting runs out of memory gracefully: external merge sort
sections.body:
Sorting seems to have the same problem: to put keys in order, surely you need them all in memory at once? An in-memory sort does, and it would fail exactly like the hash map. The trick is to never sort everything at once.

Version 2 is an **external merge sort**, and it has two phases. The stepper below runs it on twelve keys.

1. Run generation. Read as many lines as fit in a buffer of M bytes, sort them in memory, and write them to a temporary file. That sorted file is a **run**. Repeat until the input ends. N bytes of input give about N / M runs.
2. Merging. Open several runs at once and keep the current first line of each in a priority queue (a heap). Write the smallest line, read the next line from the run it came from, and repeat. This needs one line, or one read buffer, per open run, however long the runs are. The number of runs one merge reads is the **fan-in**, F. With more than F runs, merge them in groups, then merge the results: each pass turns r runs into r / F, rounded up.

Put numbers on it. 100 GB of keys with a 1 GB buffer gives 100 runs. With a fan-in of 16, the first pass leaves 7 runs and the second leaves 1: two merge passes. With a fan-in of 128, one. Each pass reads and writes the whole 100 GB, but sequentially, from the start of each file to its end. Once the keys are sorted, `uniq -c` counts them with one counter. So sorting costs more CPU (n log n comparisons) and extra disk passes, and in exchange it never runs out of memory. It just gets slower as the input grows.

GNU sort does all of this without being asked. Its options, from the coreutils manual:

| Option | What it sets | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `-S` | the buffer for run generation (also as a % of RAM) | chosen by sort |
| `-T` | where runs go (several `-T` spread them over disks) | `$TMPDIR` or `/tmp` |
| `--batch-size` | the fan-in | 16, minimum 2 |
| `--parallel` | threads for the in-memory sorting | the number of CPUs, at most 8 |
| `--compress-program` | a program that compresses runs | none |

Set `LC_ALL=C` too. The manual recommends it to get the traditional order, by byte value, and on this log it also made `sort` about five times faster than the UTF-8 locale, which compares by language rules.

In the Try it, `sort -S 4M` on 46 MB of paths wrote 73 runs. A single merge can't read 73 runs at a fan-in of 16, so sort first merged 64 of them in four groups, then merged the remaining 13 straight into the output: 77 temporary files. It never held more than about 7 MB. GNU sort also skips work the simple model does: the 9 runs left over went straight into the final merge, while the full passes of the stepper and the lab would have rewritten all 73 once more.

try.title: Count GNU sort's runs
steps: In the lab box, extract the paths into a file, then sort it with a 4 MB buffer three times, with fan-ins of 16, 64 and 2. `strace` logs the system calls a program makes, here every file `sort` opens, and `grep` counts the temporary files it created.
Before you run it: with 73 runs, predict which fan-in creates the most temporary files, and roughly how many.
Then compare the memory of `sort` with a 4 MB buffer and with its default buffer.

code.title: in the lab box
code.src:
cd /tmp
awk '{print $7}' /labs/sim/build/l02/access.log > paths.txt    # 2,000,000 keys, 46 MB
wc -lc paths.txt
export LC_ALL=C
mkdir -p runs
for b in 16 64 2; do
  strace -f -qq -e trace=openat -o trace.txt sort -S 4M --batch-size=$b -T /tmp/runs paths.txt > sorted.txt
  echo "batch-size $b: $(grep -c 'runs/sort.*O_CREAT' trace.txt) temporary files"
done
/usr/bin/time -f '%M KB max memory, %e s' sort -S 4M -T /tmp/runs paths.txt > /dev/null
/usr/bin/time -f '%M KB max memory, %e s' sort -T /tmp/runs paths.txt > /dev/null

try.expect:
```text
 2000000 46478507 paths.txt
batch-size 16: 77 temporary files
batch-size 64: 74 temporary files
batch-size 2: 144 temporary files
6836 KB max memory, 0.72 s
300564 KB max memory, 0.39 s
```

The three counts fit 73 runs. With a fan-in of 64, sort merged 64 runs into one file and then merged that file with the other 9 into the output: 73 + 1. With 16 it needed four intermediate merges: 73 + 4. With 2 it merged pairs again and again: 73 + 71. With 4 MB, `sort` stayed under 7 MB of memory. Left to choose its own buffer, it took 300 MB, wrote no temporary files at all and finished sooner. Times vary from run to run; on this laptop they moved by about 50%.

sections.h: When a laptop beats a cluster, and when it stops
sections.body:
In January 2014 Adam Drake answered a blog post by Tom Hayden, who had counted the results of chess games with Hadoop: 1.75 GB of game records on a cluster of 7 `c1.medium` machines on Amazon's Elastic MapReduce, in about 26 minutes. That is about 1.14 MB per second. Drake wrote a shell pipeline of `find`, `xargs`, `mawk` and a second `mawk` on his laptop. It processed 3.46 GB, twice the data, in about 12 seconds, about 270 MB per second. Plain `cat` of the same files into `/dev/null` ran at 272 MB per second, so his pipeline was as fast as the disk could deliver the bytes.

His headline says 235 times faster. That number assumes Hadoop would have needed twice as long for twice the data. The raw comparison is 26 minutes against 12 seconds: about 130 times faster, on twice the input. Quote the raw ratio when you use the example; it is strong enough.

His reasons map onto this lesson. The stages of a pipeline run at the same time, like a small cluster on one machine. His awk kept three counters (wins, losses, draws), hash aggregation with a tiny working set, so nothing had to be sorted. `xargs -P4` ran four awk processes on four cores. And `mawk` was faster than `gawk` for this job. The cluster, meanwhile, paid for job startup, task scheduling and moving data it didn't need to move. The What data systems are for track's lesson on growing past one machine made the same point with the COST paper: measure against one good single-threaded program before you assume you need more machines.

Your own pipeline may be bound by something else. In the last Try it below, `cat` reads the cached log at gigabytes per second, while the full pipeline manages about 100 MB per second: it is limited by sorting two million keys, not by the disk. Drake's job never sorted at all. Find the slow stage by timing the pipeline one stage longer at a time, and fix that one.

One machine stops being enough in a few clear cases. The input is bigger than the machine's disks. The job is too slow for its deadline even when it streams at disk speed: by lesson 1's formula, 10 TB at 2 GB/s is 83 minutes. A job that runs for hours has to survive a machine dying halfway. Or many teams need to run jobs over the same data. Then you need this lesson's three parts on many machines: storage spread over them, a scheduler that starts the work near the data, and a sort across machines. That is lesson 3.

try.title: Find the slow stage
steps: In the lab box, in `/labs/sim/build/l02`, time the pipeline one stage at a time: just `cat`, then `awk`, then `awk` into `sort`, then the same with `LC_ALL=C`, then the whole pipeline.
Predict before you run: which stage takes most of the time, the reading, the field extraction or the sort?

code.title: in the lab box, in /labs/sim/build/l02
code.src:
TIMEFORMAT='%R s'
time (cat access.log > /dev/null)
time (awk '{print $7}' access.log > /dev/null)
time (awk '{print $7}' access.log | sort > /dev/null)
time (awk '{print $7}' access.log | LC_ALL=C sort > /dev/null)
time (export LC_ALL=C; awk '{print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5 > /dev/null)

try.expect:
```text
0.103 s
0.508 s
8.955 s
1.797 s
2.437 s
```

Reading 231 MB took a tenth of a second, because the file was in the page cache. Extracting the field took half a second. The sort took most of the rest: about 9 seconds in the box's UTF-8 locale and under 2 seconds with `LC_ALL=C`. The whole pipeline with `LC_ALL=C` ran in about 2.4 seconds, roughly 100 MB per second. On a second run every number moved (the laptop was busy with other work), but the order of the stages didn't.

refs.title: Command-line tools can be 235x faster than your Hadoop cluster (Adam Drake, 2014)

analogy: Picture the post room of a large company on a Monday, with a mountain of letters to count by department. One way is a wall of pigeonholes, one per department: drop each letter in its hole and count the holes at the end. That is a hash map, and it's the fastest way while the wall has a hole for every department. With fifty thousand addressees instead of fifty departments, you run out of wall. The other way needs only a table. Take an armful of letters, sort it by name, and stack it. Do that until the mountain is gone, then merge the sorted stacks by always taking the smallest name from the tops, and count each name as it goes past. That is an external merge sort, and it works for any number of names. The analogy breaks in one place: a clerk can glance over a whole stack, while a merge sees only the top letter of each stack, which is exactly why it needs so little room.
in_your_world: Reconciliation is where you'll meet this. An acquirer sends a settlement file with 80 million capture lines, and you need every idempotency key that appears more than once. A Quarkus job that loads the keys into a `HashSet` passes every test with a sample of 100,000 lines and dies in production, because the working set is the distinct keys, about 80 million at roughly 100 bytes each. `cut -d, -f4 settlement.csv | LC_ALL=C sort -S 1G -T /scratch | uniq -d` finds the duplicates in bounded memory. The databases you use make the same choice for every `GROUP BY`. PostgreSQL's plans show `HashAggregate` or `Sort` followed by `GroupAggregate`, and since PostgreSQL 13 a hash aggregate that outgrows `work_mem` spills to disk instead of failing. Oracle's plans show `HASH GROUP BY` or `SORT GROUP BY`, and both spill to the temporary tablespace.
mistake: The common mistake is picking a hash map by the size of a sample instead of the number of distinct keys. A deduplication or counting job keyed by something unique (an idempotency key, a card number, a URL with ids in it) is tested on a day's sample, where the map holds a few hundred thousand entries, and then runs on a year, where it needs tens of millions. It doesn't slow down first: it runs for most of an hour and then throws `OutOfMemoryError`, with nothing written. People make it because the hash map is the obvious, fast code, and memory use isn't visible in a unit test. The fix is a line of arithmetic before the code: distinct keys times about 100 bytes plus the key length on the JVM. If that doesn't fit with plenty of room, sort first (`sort -S ... -T ...`, or an external sort in the job), or split the keys by hash into files that each fit, and count one file at a time.

compare.title: The same top five, by hashing and by sorting

a.label: Hash aggregation in awk
a.title: one pass, memory per distinct key
a.src:
awk '{n[$7]++} END {for (p in n) print n[p], p}' access.log \
  | sort -rn | head -5

# the map holds 351,305 paths until END
# 40,480 KB max memory in the lab box

b.label: Sort, then count neighbours
b.title: sorted runs, memory bounded by -S
b.src:
awk '{print $7}' access.log \
  | LC_ALL=C sort -S 4M | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5

# sort keeps a 4 MB buffer and spills runs to disk
# 6,836 KB max memory for sort -S 4M on these keys

compare.note: Both print the same five lines. The awk version keeps one entry per distinct path in a hash table: `/usr/bin/time` measured 40 MB for 351,305 paths, and it would grow with every new path. The sort version keeps a fixed buffer, writes sorted runs to temporary files and merges them, so its memory stays near the `-S` value however many distinct keys the log holds. `uniq -c` then needs one counter. The second `sort -rn` in both is small: it orders the distinct paths, not the two million lines.

worked.title: Find duplicate captures in an acquirer's file

steps.say: The acquirer's settlement file has 80 million capture lines, and the idempotency key is a 36-character UUID in column 4. Almost every key is distinct. First, estimate the hash map: distinct keys times bytes per entry.

Next, size the sort. The keys alone are about 80 million x 37 bytes (with the newline), about 3 GB. With a 256 MB buffer, run generation gives at least 12 runs. GNU sort's runs come out smaller than its buffer, because the buffer also holds bookkeeping for every line, so measure on a sample with the strace trick before you trust the count.
steps.code:
// 2. runs and merge passes, with the lab's mergePasses
val keyBytes = 80_000_000L * 37                    // 2,960,000,000 bytes, about 3 GB
val buffer = 256_000_000L
val runs = ((keyBytes + buffer - 1) / buffer).toInt()   // 12 runs, or more on GNU sort
mergePasses(runs, fanIn = 16)                     // 1: a single merge reads all 12
mergePasses(runs * 6, fanIn = 16)                 // 2: if GNU's runs come out six times smaller

steps.say: Write the job as a pipeline: map to the key column, sort with a fixed buffer and a scratch disk, and let `uniq -d` print one copy of each key that occurs more than once. `LC_ALL=C` gives byte order and a faster sort.
steps.code:
# 3. bounded memory, sequential disk I/O
cut -d, -f4 settlement-2026-11-06.csv \
  | LC_ALL=C sort -S 256M -T /scratch --parallel=4 \
  | uniq -d > duplicate-keys.txt

steps.say: Check the result against the arithmetic, not just for being non-empty: the output is sorted, and every key in it must appear at least twice in the input. A key from the file that `grep -c` counts once is a bug in the pipeline, not a duplicate.
steps.code:
# 4. spot-check one reported key
head -1 duplicate-keys.txt
grep -c "$(head -1 duplicate-keys.txt)" settlement-2026-11-06.csv   # 2 or more

lab.title: Count a log by hashing and by sorting
steps: From the `labs` folder, run the tests. All fourteen fail with `NotImplementedError`. `AccessLog.kt` is finished: it generates the same seeded log as the Try its. Read `ExternalSorter.sort` in `ExternalSort.kt` too; it calls the two pieces you'll write and counts the passes.
In `Pipeline.kt`, write `field` (awk's `$n`) and `countAdjacent` (`uniq -c`). The `PipelineTest` checks that unsorted input splits a key, then runs the whole pipeline on 100,000 lines.
In `HashCounter.kt`, write `add`. A new key is charged `entryBytes`; if that would pass the budget, throw `MemoryBudgetExceeded` and change nothing.

In `ExternalSort.kt`, write `mergePasses`, then `writeRuns` and `mergeGroup`. Use `store.write` and `store.open`: the tests read the store's counters to check how many runs you wrote and how many files you held open at once.

Run the tests until all fourteen pass. The last `ExternalSortTest` runs both counters on 200,000 lines: the hash counter fails in 1 MB, and the sort, holding 5,000 lines at a time, gives exactly the same counts.
hints: `line.split(' ', '\t').filter { it.isNotEmpty() }` gives awk's fields; `getOrNull(n - 1)` handles short lines.
In `add`, look the key up first. Only a missing key costs memory, and the budget check must come before you change `bytesUsed` or the map.
`mergePasses` is a loop: while more than one run is left, `runs = (runs + fanIn - 1) / fanIn` and count a pass.

`keys.chunked(runSize)` holds one batch at a time. For the merge, a `PriorityQueue<Pair<String, Int>>` of (line, reader index) ordered by line; pass `store.write` a `sequence { }` that polls the smallest line, yields it and refills from the same reader. Close the readers and delete the inputs in a `finally`.

drill.title: Write the k-way merge from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write a function that merges several sorted lists of strings into one sorted list using a priority queue, holding only one element per input at a time. Then say how many passes a fan-in of 10 needs for 250 runs.

recap: `awk '{print $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` is a complete batch job on one machine: awk maps each line to a key, the first sort brings equal keys together, `uniq -c` reduces each group.
`uniq` only compares a line with the one before it, so without the sort its counts are silently wrong.
The Unix style (small programs, one text interface, wiring kept outside the programs) is what MapReduce copied, with files in a distributed file system in place of pipes.
Hash aggregation counts in one pass and wins while the distinct keys fit in memory; on the JVM an entry costs about 100 bytes plus the key, and past the heap it fails all at once.

An external merge sort writes sorted runs of buffer size and merges them F at a time: about N / M runs and ceil(log_F(runs)) passes, each a full sequential read and write. GNU sort does it by itself (`-S`, `-T`, `--batch-size` 16, `--parallel` up to 8; set `LC_ALL=C`).

A laptop pipeline beat a 7-node Hadoop cluster by about 130 times on the raw numbers. One machine stops being enough when the data outgrows its disks or its deadline, or the job must survive a machine failing.

quiz.q: A teammate runs `awk '{print $9}' access.log | uniq -c` to count status codes and reports that 201 appears 1, 2 or 3 times at most. What went wrong?
options: `uniq -c` caps its counts at a small number by default
The input wasn't sorted, so `uniq` counted only runs of neighbouring equal lines
The log is too big for `uniq`, which needs a hash table
quiz.why: `uniq` compares each line only with the previous one, so on unsorted input every interruption starts a new count and a code appears on thousands of output lines with small counts. Adding `sort` before `uniq -c` brings equal codes together. `uniq` needs almost no memory and has no cap; that's exactly why it depends on sorted input.

quiz.q: A job counts events per card over a year: 4 billion lines and 300 million distinct cards. It runs on a JVM with a 16 GB heap. Which plan fits?
options: A `HashMap<String, Long>`, since 4 billion lines need only 300 million entries
Load the year into memory and call `sorted()`
An external merge sort (or hash-partitioning into files) followed by a streaming count
Any of them, because the JVM will spill the map to disk
quiz.why: 300 million entries at roughly 100 bytes plus the key is over 30 GB, about twice the heap. Sorting in memory needs the 4 billion lines at once, which is worse. An external sort holds only its buffer, and partitioning the keys by hash into files that each fit lets a hash map count one file at a time. A JVM `HashMap` never spills to disk; it throws `OutOfMemoryError`.

quiz.q: A sort of 400 GB uses a 2 GB buffer and a fan-in of 16. How many merge passes does it need after run generation?
quiz.why: 400 GB / 2 GB gives 200 runs. One pass merges groups of 16, leaving ceil(200 / 16) = 13 runs, and a second pass merges those 13 into one: 2 passes. One pass would need a fan-in of at least 200. 200 is the run count, not the pass count, and 8 would be about right for a fan-in of 2.

quiz.q: Adam Drake's laptop pipeline processed 3.46 GB in about 12 seconds; the Hadoop job processed 1.75 GB in about 26 minutes. What is the raw speed-up, and why is it the one to quote?
options: About 235 times, because that is the published headline
About 2 times, because the laptop read twice the data
About 130 times: 26 minutes against 12 seconds, measured on the jobs as they ran
It can't be compared, because the inputs differ
quiz.why: 1,560 seconds divided by 12 is 130, comparing the two runs as measured. The 235x headline assumes Hadoop would have taken twice as long on twice the data, a reasonable guess that nobody measured. Quoting the raw number keeps the claim honest, and it's still two orders of magnitude.

quiz.q: From lesson 1: a nightly job must sort 6 TB of keys, and one machine's disks stream at 2 GB/s. A sort with one merge pass reads the input, writes the runs, reads them back and writes the output. Ignoring CPU, about how long does that take on one machine?
quiz.why: Four full trips over 6 TB move 24 TB. At 2 GB/s that is 12,000 seconds, about 3 hours 20 minutes. 50 minutes counts only one read of the input; the runs must be written and read back too. If the deadline is two hours, this is the case where one machine stops being enough, or where you must read fewer bytes first.

flashcards.back: `uniq` compares each line only with the line before it, so it can only count copies that are next to each other. Sorting makes equal keys neighbours.

flashcards.front: What does a hash aggregation's memory depend on?
flashcards.back: The number of distinct keys, not the number of lines. On the JVM each entry costs about 100 bytes plus the key.

flashcards.front: What are the two phases of an external merge sort?
flashcards.back: Run generation: sort chunks that fit in the buffer and write each as a sorted run. Merging: read F runs at once through a priority queue and write one sorted run, repeating until one is left.

flashcards.front: How many merge passes do R runs need with fan-in F?
flashcards.back: ceil(log_F(R)): each pass turns r runs into ceil(r / F). 100 runs need 2 passes at F = 16 and 1 at F = 128.

flashcards.front: GNU sort's defaults for fan-in and threads?
flashcards.back: `--batch-size` (fan-in) 16, minimum 2. `--parallel` is the number of CPUs, at most 8. `-S` sets the buffer, `-T` the temp directory.

flashcards.front: What happens to a pipeline when `head` exits early?
flashcards.back: The program writing into the pipe gets SIGPIPE on its next write and stops, so the rest of the input is never read.

flashcards.front: Drake's laptop vs Hadoop, raw numbers?
flashcards.back: 3.46 GB in about 12 s on a laptop against 1.75 GB in about 26 minutes on 7 machines: about 130 times faster raw (the 235x headline scales Hadoop to the same data).

terms.plain: A job that reads existing input without changing it and computes its whole output from scratch, so a bad run can just be rerun.
A kernel buffer that connects one program's output to the next program's input, with both programs running at the same time.
A slow consumer slowing down its producer: a writer blocks when the pipe's buffer is full.
Grouping or counting with a hash table keyed by the group: one pass, memory per distinct key.
Sorting data bigger than memory by writing sorted runs to disk and merging them a few at a time.
A sorted temporary file written by one round of an external sort.
How many runs one merge reads at once; GNU sort's `--batch-size`.

explain_back.prompt: A colleague asks why `sort | uniq -c` can count a 500 GB log on a laptop with 16 GB of RAM, while their Kotlin `HashMap` version of the same count died with `OutOfMemoryError` on a 50 GB log. Explain both, and say when the `HashMap` is the better choice.
explain_back.answer: The HashMap keeps one entry per distinct key until the last line is read, and on the JVM each entry costs about 100 bytes plus the key. If the 50 GB log has a few hundred million distinct keys, that is tens of GB of heap, so it dies, and it dies late, after doing most of the work. `sort` never holds everything. It reads a buffer's worth of lines, sorts them, writes them to a temporary file as a sorted run, and repeats. Then it merges the runs, reading a handful at a time and keeping only the current line of each in memory. Its memory stays near the buffer size whatever the input size; it just needs disk space for the runs and takes longer, because each merge pass reads and writes the data again. Once sorted, equal keys are neighbours and `uniq -c` counts them with one counter. The HashMap is the better choice when the distinct keys fit comfortably in memory, such as counts per endpoint, merchant or status: it makes one pass, does no sorting and touches no disk.

deeper.body:
Real engines don't choose once between hashing and sorting; they start with a hash table and fall back when it fills. One classic fallback is **hash partitioning**. When the table is full, split the keys by a second hash function into, say, 64 partition files on disk, so that each partition holds about a 64th of the distinct keys. Then aggregate one partition at a time, each with its own hash table that now fits. Every key lands in exactly one partition, so the per-partition results never need merging. It costs one extra write and read of the data, like one merge pass. Database textbooks call the join version a Grace hash join.

PostgreSQL took this route in version 13: a `HashAggregate` that outgrows `work_mem` now writes the groups it can't hold to disk in partitions and processes them afterwards, where older versions could use far more memory than planned. Spark's hash aggregate falls back the other way: when its map runs out of memory, it sorts what it has, spills it to disk, and finishes with a merge, so the hash table is the fast path and the sort is the safety net.

The map step can also shrink the problem before any of this. If each of four `awk` processes counts its own quarter of the file in a small hash map, and a last step adds up the four sets of counts, the expensive part only sees a few rows per key per process. That is MapReduce's combiner, and the next lesson builds it. DDIA's second edition, chapter 11, walks through the same log pipeline and the same hash-versus-sort trade-off, then follows it onto a cluster.
